bib.title: Introduction to Information Retrieval, Chapter 3: Dictionaries and tolerant retrieval
bib.venue: Cambridge University Press (online edition, draft April 1, 2009)

question: How can an inverted index's vocabulary be searched robustly under wildcards, spelling errors and phonetic variation?
contributions: Wildcard handling with permuterm and k-gram indexes
Spelling correction by edit distance, k-gram overlap and context-sensitive enumeration

results.claim: A permuterm index (all rotations of each term plus $) can cause almost a ten-fold space increase for an English dictionary.
results.setup: Permuterm index versus plain dictionary, English terms; no measurement shown, asserted
results.quote: this can represent an almost ten-fold space increase

results.claim: Jaccard coefficient of query bord against vocabulary term boardroom over bigrams is 2/(8+3-2).
results.setup: 2-gram index, q=bord (3 bigrams), t=boardroom (8 bigrams), 2 postings hits (bo, rd); equals 2/9, not printed as a decimal
results.note: Bigram counts exclude the $ boundary marker here, unlike the 3-gram castle example on p.54 which includes $.

results.claim: Edit distance between cat and dog is 3.
results.note: Sentence is split across lines in the text: 'the edit distance be-' / 'tween cat and dog is 3'.

results.claim: Dynamic-programming edit distance costs O(|s1| x |s2|) time.
results.setup: Weighted or unit-weight edit distance between two strings, Fig 3.5 algorithm

results.claim: Balanced binary search tree dictionary lookup takes O(log M) comparisons.
results.setup: Balanced binary tree over M vocabulary terms
results.quote: number of comparisons that is O(log M)

results.claim: Hermann maps to soundex code H655.
results.setup: Soundex variant described on p.64 (keep first letter, vowels/H/W/Y to 0, consonant classes to digits, collapse repeats, drop zeros, pad to 4)

results.claim: Zobel and Dart (1995) found k-gram indexing very effective for candidate generation but needing a finer technique such as edit distance.
results.setup: Empirical study of several spelling-correction methods; no numbers given in the chapter

results.claim: Zobel and Dart (1996) found a soundex variant poor for general spelling correction while pronunciation-based phonetic algorithms perform well.
results.setup: Evaluation of phonetic matching algorithms; no numbers given
results.quote: algorithm performs poorly for general spelling correction

results.claim: Noisy-channel models are described as state-of-the-art for spelling correction as of 2008.
results.setup: Probabilistic spelling correction (Kernighan 1990, Brill and Moore 2000)
results.quote: Many would regard them as the state-of-the-art approach.

results.claim: Spell-correction exposure options: always, only if term not in dictionary, only if fewer than a preset number of results (say fewer than five), or as a Did-you-mean suggestion.
results.setup: Four ways of exposing spelling correction in the UI; threshold five is an example, not a recommendation

results.claim: Exposing wildcard search in the main interface encourages unneeded use and raises engine load.
results.quote: increasing the processing load on the search engine

limits: Pre-neural (2008): no embedding or learned-model query rewriting, no LLM query parsing; noisy-channel models called state-of-the-art.
Chapter gives almost no measured numbers; ten-fold permuterm blowup is asserted, empirical comparisons are only cited (Zobel and Dart).
Soundex is writing-system dependent; fails on Wade-Giles j vs Pinyin r and is aimed at proper nouns, European languages.
Isolated-term correction misses real-word errors such as 'flew form Heathrow'; context-sensitive enumeration can be combinatorially expensive.
Search trees need a prescribed character ordering.
Edit-distance treatment fixes equal weights though weighted edits are said to be very effective in practice.
practices: Use a B-tree for dictionary lookup, especially when part is disk-resident; choose a,b from disk block size (p.51).
Handle a single-* wildcard with a regular B-tree plus a reverse B-tree and intersect (p.52).
For general wildcards use permuterm or k-gram index, then post-filter candidates against the original pattern (pp.53-55).
Treat Boolean combinations of wildcards as conjunction of disjunctions (p.55).
Hide wildcard functionality behind an advanced interface to limit load (p.56).
Break spelling ties by choosing the more common term, by collection counts or by query-log frequency (p.57).
Generate candidates with a k-gram index, then rank by edit distance (p.62).
For context-sensitive correction, keep only the most frequent biword combinations from collection or query logs (p.62).
Use phonetic hashing for proper-noun searches (p.63).

terms.definition: a query using * to mean any (possibly empty) string of characters
an inverted index in which all rotations of each term augmented with $ link to the original vocabulary term
a dictionary of all k-grams occurring in any vocabulary term, each posting list pointing to the terms containing it
the minimum number of edit operations (insert, delete, replace) required to transform s1 into s2
correcting a single query term at a time, even in multi-term queries
correcting terms using their neighbouring query terms, e.g. flew form Heathrow
phonetic hash turning each term into a 4-character code (letter plus three digits)
